newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban vow to hold Kabul, defy ultimatum to quit.
newsitem.headline: Taleban vow to hold Kabul, defy ultimatum to quit.

text.p: Afghanistan's new rulers, the radical Islamic Taleban, have defied a quit-or-else ultimatum from the ousted government and vowed to fend off any assault on the capital Kabul they seized nearly three weeks ago.

Taleban, which controls some three-quarters of the country, rejected a demand from the military chief in the previous administration of President Burhanuddin Rabbani and bombed his forces north of Kabul.
Ex-defence minister Ahmad Shah Masood told the new power in Kabul to pull all its fighters out of the capital or face the consequences.
But Taleban, which has imposed strict Islamic rule in the capital, remained defiant, ordering warplanes to raid Masood's forces on plains north of Kabul on Wednesday.
Acting information minister Amir Khan Mutaqi ruled out an evacuation of Kabul. "We have enough power to defend our government, our people in Kabul by the aid of God," he said.

Masood, whose forces have pushed Taleban out of two towns north of the capital, demanded the purist Islamic movement withdraw from the city it captured on September 27 or face bloodshed and destruction.
A similar call was heard at the United Nations Security Council in New York.

The ousted government's deputy Foreign Minister Abdul Rahim Ghafoorzai urged Taleban to evacuate Kabul and proposed an international police force to ensure security before negotiations on an interim government of national unity.
Unless these proposals were accepted, the Afghan armed forces would "resort to action to end this catastrophic situation" in Kabul, Ghafoorzai told the Security Council.
He spoke at the start of a debate requested by Russia and several Central Asian republics concerned by the upsurge of fighting near their southern borders.

Moscow's U.N. envoy Sergei Lavrov said Russia considered "the approach of the flames of war in neighbouring Afghanistan toward the borders of the Commonwealth (of Independent States)" as a direct threat to its national interests and security and to stability in the region.
The Security Council debate was adjourned without a decision late on Wednesday.
Reflecting the fears across the region, two neighbours of the Central Asian state, Iran and Pakistan, made separate moves for a negotiated peace.
Iranian Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati said in the Kazakh capital Almaty that the crisis in Afghanistan could not be resolved by force and called on all factions to negotiate.
Shi'ite Moslem Iran has criticised the Sunni Moslem Taleban, saying its attempts to impose a harsh version of Islamic Sharia law are giving Islam a bad name.

Pakistan sent Interior Minister Naseerullah Babar for peace talks between Taleban's acting foreign minister Mullah Mohammad Ghaus and powerful northern warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum, Afghan sources said.

The four-hour meeting at Qala-i-Jangi fort outside Mazar-i-Sharif decided to resume talks on Thursday on the proposed formation of a commission to settle the country's political future, a spokesman for Dostum said.
Pakistan, denying charges that it supports the Taleban, offered to set up peace talks between the Afghan warring sides after Dostum aligned himself with Rabbani against the Taleban.
Taleban warplanes bombed the strategic town of Jabal os-Siraj, held by Masood forces, for a second successive day, witnesses said.

In Geneva, the International Committee of the Red Cross said at least 800 people have been wounded in recent fighting in Afghanistan and hospitals are full of victims from the frontline north of Kabul.

Masood has swept out of his Panjsher valley stronghold some 80 km (60 miles) north of Kabul, rolling Taleban forces back across the plain north of the capital in the past week and taking the towns of Jabal os-Siraj and Charikar.
Reuters reporter Kurt Schork reported from Jabal os-Siraj late on Tuesday that despite the shifting front line, Masood's lightning advance towards the capital appears to have largely halted.
Masood's position strengthened on Monday when the northern Uzbek leader Dostum recognised the ousted government of Rabbani.
But there was no immediate sign of Dostum's forces entering the battle and no sign of any impending assault on the city, which was calm on Wednesday.
